title: Is the email credential set on the live site?
why: Invoice email is finished code that returns quietly when it has no credential, so nothing reports a failure — the app just says “queued”. The deploy log says the credential was never set, but that log stops on 4 July and I cannot see the live secret list. This is the only item on the page that may be losing something right now.

options.label: Leave it — email isn’t part of 1.0
options.consequence: Honest, and it means saying so in the app rather than showing “queued”. Overdue chasing goes with it.

options.label: I’ll check, and set it if it’s missing
options.consequence: Two minutes in the hosting dashboard. It is the cheapest thing on this page and the only one where waiting has an ongoing cost.
options.because: It is two minutes of your time, and it is the only thing here with a cost that is running right now.

options.label: Give me access and I’ll do it
options.consequence: Faster for you, but it means handing over a credential store, which is a bigger decision than the one being made here.

note_hint: If it is already set, say so and I will stop reporting it as a risk.

title: Recurring invoices: back on now, or proven first?
why: It was switched off on 28 June after billing one client 41 times in a night. A duplicate guard went in afterwards and has only ever run against test data. The call on 11 August already leaned towards proving it before 1.0 goes out.

options.label: Switch it back on now
options.consequence: Scheduled invoices resume today. The guard is written and reviewed but has never met real data, and the last surprise here was a client receiving 41 invoices.

options.label: Prove the guard first
options.consequence: A day’s work replaying one real schedule against a copy of the data. It is what the call agreed, and the failure it protects against was visible to a client.
options.because: The bug cost one client 41 invoices in a night. Proving the guard is a day; being wrong twice is worse than being a day late.

options.label: Leave it off for 1.0
options.consequence: Ships sooner with one fewer moving part. The feature stays written and switched off, which is what the roadmap already calls shipped.

note_hint: If there is a client you would rather not be the test case, name them.

title: Which tax rounding rule should Kettle use?
why: Three rules are defensible and they disagree by cents on every invoice with more than one line. This is the last thing blocking the final roadmap feature, and it is a question about what your invoices should say rather than about code.

options.label: Round each line, then add up
options.consequence: What Xero does. Picking this keeps your invoices matching your accounting software to the cent, which matters more than matching a worked example.

options.label: Add the lines up, then round
options.consequence: What the tax office’s own worked examples do for Australian dollars. Recommended on that basis — if you reconcile against Xero rather than the ATO examples, the next option is the right one and I would change my answer.
options.because: It is what the tax office publishes, so it is the rule you can point at if a client ever queries a figure.

options.label: Round to the other currency’s smallest unit
options.consequence: Most correct-looking to a client abroad, and it disagrees with both of the above, so your books and your invoices will differ.

note_hint: If you reconcile against a particular accounting system, name it — that decides this.

title: Pay for live exchange rates, or cut multi-currency from 1.0?
why: Free rate feeds are once-a-day and do not cover the pair you need during the day. The one that does is $29 a month, forever, for a feature two clients have asked about.

options.label: Use the free daily rate
options.consequence: No cost, and invoices are priced on yesterday’s rate. Fine for small amounts and wrong in a way clients notice on large ones.

options.label: Pay the $29 a month
options.consequence: Multi-currency lands in 1.0 for a running cost of $348 a year, which starts before the first client uses it.

options.label: Cut it from 1.0
options.consequence: 1.0 goes out with the nine features that work. Nothing is thrown away — the conversion code stays, switched off, and this becomes a decision you make when a client actually needs it.
options.because: A wrong rate is a wrong invoice, and the free feeds do not say when they were last right.

note_hint: A ceiling, or the number of clients that would make it worth it.

title: The client portal — in 1.0, after it, or not at all?
why: It came up on the call as the difference between an invoicing script and a product people pay for. Nothing exists for it, and it is the largest single piece of work anyone has proposed. Nothing in the repository measures whether clients would use it — so this is appetite and scope, which is yours, and I have deliberately not put a recommendation on it.

options.label: After 1.0
options.consequence: 1.0 ships on the roadmap it already has. This is weeks of work and a public surface to defend, decided on an opinion rather than on a number.

options.label: In 1.0
options.consequence: 1.0 becomes the product rather than the tool, and slips by weeks. Worth it if the thing being launched to is a paying audience.

options.label: Drop it
options.consequence: It stops coming up. Straightforward to revisit — nothing has been built either way.

note_hint: If a specific client has asked for this, that changes the answer.

title: Chasing overdue invoices — in 1.0?
why: Two days of work, and it cannot be trusted at all until invoice email actually sends in production. Its value is the most direct of anything on this page: it is the feature that gets you paid sooner.

options.label: Out of 1.0
options.consequence: One less thing between here and shipping. The invoices still go out; nothing follows them up.

options.label: Yes, once email is confirmed working
options.consequence: Two days, and it depends entirely on the credential question above. Recommended only if you answered that one; on its own it would ship a feature that silently does nothing.
options.because: It is the smallest version that is still useful, and it does not commit you to a tone of voice before you have seen one go out.

options.label: In 1.0 either way
options.consequence: Builds it now and trusts the email question gets sorted. If it does not, the nudges quietly go nowhere, which is the failure already on this page once.

note_hint: If seven, fourteen and thirty days are the wrong intervals, say what you would use.

title: Anything else you want changed before 1.0?
why: The page is built from what the repository and the call notes say. Anything you know that they do not has no other way onto it.
